title: Choose the Right Structure — short paper

criteria.name: Thesis & Choice of Structure
criteria.description: Does the paper name one operation and the structure it recommends for it, and argue that choice throughout?
criteria.present_when: A sentence states which data structure the paper recommends and for which operation.

levels.4: A specific, arguable thesis names the operation and the recommended structure; every section advances it.
levels.3: A clear thesis names the operation and the structure; the argument mostly stays on it.
levels.2: A recommendation is present but vague — e.g. 'X is better' — without naming the operation it is better for.
levels.1: No real thesis: the paper describes structures without recommending one for a specific operation.

criteria.name: Correctness of Running-Time Analysis
criteria.description: Are the running-time claims correct according to the course reading, and does the paper say which kind of guarantee each one is?
criteria.present_when: The paper gives a big-O running time for the key operation in the recommended structure and in at least one alternative.

levels.4: Every running-time claim matches the course reading, and the paper distinguishes worst-case, amortized, and expected guarantees where they differ — e.g. adding to the end of an ArrayStack is O(1) amortized because of resize(), not O(1) worst-case.
levels.3: Claims match the course reading, with one guarantee type left unstated or one minor imprecision — e.g. 'average' where the reading says 'expected'.
levels.2: Mostly correct, but one claim contradicts the course reading, or correct running times are asserted with no explanation.
levels.1: Two or more claims contradict the course reading — e.g. constant-time access to the i-th element of a linked list (the reading gives O(1 + min{i, n − i}) for DLList), or constant-time insertion into the middle of an array (O(1 + n − i) for ArrayStack).

criteria.name: Evidence & Scenario
criteria.description: Is the argument grounded in a concrete scenario, with claims backed by analysis or by the course reading?
criteria.present_when: The paper describes at least one concrete program or task, and refers to the course reading at least once.

levels.4: A concrete scenario carries the argument, the analysis is applied to it (e.g. total cost over a whole input stream), and the reading is cited where it supports a claim.
levels.3: A concrete scenario with supporting analysis; the reading is referenced, but loosely.
levels.2: A scenario is mentioned but not analyzed, or claims rest on assertion rather than evidence.
levels.1: Generic claims only: no scenario and no reference to the reading.

criteria.name: Trade-offs & Limits
criteria.description: Does the paper say where its recommended structure is the worse choice?
criteria.present_when: The paper names at least one situation in which the recommended structure is the worse choice.

levels.4: Names a specific case where the recommended structure loses, and explains why in running-time or memory terms.
levels.3: Names a case where the recommendation loses, with a brief reason.
levels.2: Acknowledges limits in general terms only — 'it depends'.
levels.1: Claims the structure is the best choice in all or most situations.

criteria.name: Clarity & Structure
criteria.description: Is the paper organized and readable for a peer?
criteria.present_when: The paper has an introduction that states its claim, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

levels.4: Tight structure and clean prose; easy to follow throughout.
levels.3: Well organized; an occasional awkward passage.
levels.2: Understandable, but disorganized or repetitive in places.
